10.0.0.en: 1 Israel is a spreading vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images. 2 Their heart is divided; now shall they be punished: he shall break down their altars, he shall spoil their images. 3 For now they shall say, We have no king, because we feared not the LORD; what then should a king do to us? 4 They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field. 5 The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven: for the people thereof shall mourn over it, and the priests thereof shall tremble for the glory thereof, because it is departed from it. 6 It shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to an enemy king: Ephraim shall receive shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel. 7 As for Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water. 8 The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

10.0.1.en: God uses many similes to reveal the extent of the corruption of the people when they deviate from God, or the extent of the corruption of the human soul by its apostasy from its Savior. He likened His people to a woman beloved of her friend, and an adulteress (Hos 3:1), a stubborn heifer (Hos 4:16), a lamb feeding in a large place for slaughter (Hos 4:16), those who remove the bound (Hos 5:10), an oven heated by the baker (Hos 7:4), a cake not turned (Hos 7:8), a silly dove without heart (Hos 7:11), a wild ass alone by himself (Hos 8:9), a bird from the birth and from the womb and from the conception (Hos 9:11), Tyre planted in a pleasant place (Hos 9:13), one who feedeth on wind and followeth after the east wind (Hos 12:1)... And here He likens them to the vine for which He provided every possibility of fruitfulness in abundance, but it bore fruit not for Him but for sin and abominations. He says: "Israel is a spreading vine (a grapevine), he bringeth forth fruit unto himself" [1]. It is a spreading vine, and as it is in the Septuagint, "a vine with good branches, its fruit abundant." It is without excuse, for He created it with a good nature and gave it the power to grow, so that it had many branches bearing its fruit, yet it brought forth the fruit for itself, that is, for its own thinking and not in submission to the true Vinedresser.

10.0.2.en: How wondrous! As much as God gives us possibilities and energies, we use them not for the glory of His name but by our own thinking for the sake of the evil lusts of our flesh, as He says: "according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images (statues)" [1]. Thus man repays God's generosity and tenderness with ingratitude.

10.1.0.en: "Their heart is divided" [2]: some deviated to one god, and others to another god, and so their hearts were torn; or perhaps their hearts were divided between the love of lusts connected with the worship of Baal and the desire to ease their consciences by practicing the worship of the living God in a formal way without spirit, so that they halted between the two parties. Their heart was no longer upright; therefore they cry to God, but not with all their heart, and so they do not find Him... for a divided heart cannot meet the Holy One or know Him.

10.2.0.en: The divisions of the inner heart rob it of the fear of the Lord, which has its consequences in the life of the community and of every member in it. As for the community, they lose the fear of the Lord and consequently lose their submission even to temporal authority, so that they have no leader able to manage their affairs, for He says: "For now they shall say, We have no king, because we feared not the LORD; what then should a king do to us?" [3]. As for the individual member, when through the divisions of his heart he loses the fear of the Lord, he loses his true holy will in the Lord, which is symbolized by the king, and so man behaves like one without a will, living in humiliation to every lust and in submission to evil habits, unable to make a spiritual decision in the Lord to be freed from the devil's enslavement of him... He behaves like one without a king. On the contrary, the believer who is pure in heart, without division, bears authority like a spiritual king, saying to this thought to enter, and it enters, and to that one to go out, and it goes out; by the Lord he controls with power his thoughts, his sights, his feelings and his emotions.

10.3.0.en: When man loses his spiritual authority and his kingly (heavenly) nature, he turns from a man of God who works into a man of words... "They have spoken words, swearing falsely in making a covenant: thus judgment springeth up as hemlock in the furrows of the field" [4]. They turn into men of words without work, and when they feel their weakness they confirm their words with false oaths that they do not keep, and they make covenants that they break, so that judgment becomes like a plowed, tilled field that grows bitter hemlock. Thus when they gather in the centers of justice (the courts), all swear falsely and make promises and do not keep them, and the places of security turn into bitterness of soul.

10.4.0.en: So it is with the spreading vine to which God gave many possibilities for bearing fruit: if it curls up around itself to bear fruit for the "ego" and for Baal, refusing to give fruit to the true Vinedresser, it loses the fear of the Lord and enters into a division of the heart, which ends in its being deprived of the king, that is, the holy will, and all authority is taken from it. The matter does not stop there, but its life turns into lamentation and trembling as it loses its inner glory and sees the gods it chose for itself collapse before its eyes. The prophet says: "The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven (vanity): for the people thereof shall mourn over it, and the priests thereof shall tremble for the glory thereof, because it is departed from it" [5]. What does he mean by this statement? The inhabitants of the capital, that is, Samaria, look at the calves of Beth-aven, or the house of vanity, and see that it has lost its glory, since the people fell under distress and the calves could not save them; so the people of Samaria fear that what befell Beth-aven will befall them, and the priests are terrified because they lose their dignity and forfeit the offerings.

10.5.0.en: When the people of Samaria lost their hope in Baal, instead of returning to God with repentance, declaring their sins, they go to the king of Assyria with gifts to appease him, in shame and disgrace... "It shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to an enemy king" [6].

10.5.1.en: What is the end of this deviating vine? "Ephraim shall receive shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel. As for Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water. The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us" [6-8].

10.5.2.en: In brief, we say that its end comes down to the following:

10.5.3.en: A. "Ephraim shall receive shame"... The tribe that led the movement to spread idol worship becomes ashamed and disgraced before the rest of the tribes, as the gods appear weak before the enemy.

10.5.4.en: B. "Israel shall be ashamed of his own counsel": since Israel proposed to appease the king of Assyria with gifts, it is ashamed when it sees Assyria humiliating it and treating it with contempt.

10.5.5.en: C. "As for Samaria, her king is cut off as the foam upon the water": the kings of Samaria, who split from the house of David in strength and might, became like bubbles on the water, and their kingdom ends in captivity under the authority of Assyria. This is the end of every division or schism, for however many vines man obtains at the beginning, his life ends like bubbles on the face of the water.

10.5.6.en: D. "The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed"; what were in their eyes high places that no one could approach is laid waste, and the glory of the golden calves of Beth-aven collapses, and instead of the banquets that were held there, ruin comes.

10.5.7.en: E. Man falls under the curse, as "the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars"; but on the great day of the Lord they say "to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us," for "it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Heb 10:36), and as it is said in the book of Revelation: "And they say to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: for the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?" (Rev 6:16-17).

10.6.0.en: 9 "O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah: there they stood: the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity did not overtake them. 10 When I desire, I will chastise them; and peoples shall be gathered against them when they are bound to their two iniquities. 11 And Ephraim is as an heifer that is taught, and loveth to tread out the corn; but I passed over upon her fair neck: I will make Ephraim to ride; Judah shall plow, and Jacob shall break his clods.

10.6.1.en: God assures us that its corruption did not stop at outward appearance, but touches its inner life; therefore the remedy must also enter into the depth of its nature. He says: "O Israel, thou hast sinned from the days of Gibeah" [9]. It is a long period of more than six centuries during which war was continually waged between the tribes and one another, that is, the danger was not from an external enemy but from inner corruption, and we saw that the men of Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin, did evil with the daughter of Israel (Judg 19-20). Therefore, if God disciplines them with distress from without, it is not fitting for them to fix their eyes on the distress, but on the inner corruption, so that they may be sanctified by the Lord and He may save them from the distress. "When I desire, I will chastise them; and peoples shall be gathered against them when they are bound to their two iniquities" [10].

10.7.0.en: Finally He explains how Israel became content with inner humiliation and bowed its neck to the yoke of sin, so that it became like the trained heifer that loves to thresh, bearing the yoke in order to eat from what it threshes [11].

10.8.s.en: 3. The need for a new sowing

10.8.0.en: 12 "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to goodness, break up for yourselves a plowing, for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and teach you righteousness. 13 Ye have plowed hypocrisy, ye have reaped iniquity, ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men. 14 Therefore shall a tumult arise among thy people, and all thy fortresses shall be spoiled, as Shalman spoiled Betharbel in the day of battle: the mother was dashed in pieces upon her children. 15 So shall Bethel do unto you because of your great wickedness: in a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off.

10.8.1.en: If the vine has become barren because of its inner corruption, there is an urgent need for a new sowing that the Lord Himself plants, giving us the fruit of knowledge and righteousness, for He says: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap according to goodness, break up for yourselves a plowing, for it is time to seek the LORD, till he come and teach you righteousness" [12]. The Septuagint puts it more clearly: "Sow to yourselves in righteousness, reap the fruit of life, be enlightened with the light of knowledge, seek the Lord until He brings you the fruit of righteousness." If the Lord Christ is "our righteousness," then the time has become suitable for the new sowing, in which the Lord Christ dwells in us, as though He is planted within us to renew our nature, so that we bear the fruit of life, and He opens our eyes by His Holy Spirit so that our insight is enlightened. Thus He affirms, "seek the Lord until He brings you the fruit of righteousness," for the righteousness we receive is not from ourselves but is the work of the Lord in us.

10.8.2.en: But God does not work in the lazy and the slack; therefore He says: "Sow... reap... be enlightened... seek," affirming our positive role so that we may receive God's work in us. Father Nesteros comments on the phrase "be enlightened with the light of knowledge," saying: [You must persevere with striving in reading, which I see you doing, while seeking with all longing to attain practical, experiential knowledge first, that is, knowledge of conduct, for without it the theoretical purity of which we speak cannot be acquired.]

10.9.0.en: Let us seek the Lord Himself, who comes to us with the fruit of His righteousness, and let us not rely on ourselves or our human possibilities, lest we hear the words of rebuke: "Ye have plowed hypocrisy, ye have reaped iniquity, ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men" [13]. He who relies on his own way or depends on the multitude of his mighty men is plowing hypocrisy, reaping iniquity and eating lies. Israel relied on its own counsel without returning to God, and so caused the people tumult and disturbance, and lost its fortresses, and its women and children fell under the cruelty of Shalmaneser king of Assyria. "Therefore shall a tumult arise among thy people (loss of peace), and all thy fortresses shall be spoiled (loss of security), as Shalman (Shalmaneser) spoiled Betharbel in the day of battle: the mother was dashed in pieces upon her children" [14]. So every man who relies on himself, his life turns into tumult, and he loses his spiritual fortresses and becomes plunder to the devil, who takes him captive as Shalmaneser took many captive.

10.10.0.en: He ends his speech with a threat: "So shall Bethel do unto you because of your great wickedness: in a morning shall the king of Israel utterly be cut off" [15]. It is as though He says that what befalls you is not the doing of the king of Assyria, but the doing of Bethel, which became a snare for you, catching you for pagan abominations. Do not rely on the king of Israel, for he perishes in the morning, that is, he is defeated at the beginning of the battle, falls and does not rise!

11.0.0.en: 1 "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt. 2 As they called them, so they went from them: they sacrificed unto Baalim, and burned incense to graven images. 3 I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them. 4 I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them.

11.0.1.en: At the beginning of this chapter God speaks of Israel, that is, His people, or the human soul, as representing a child beloved by God. He longs to release him from the bondage of Pharaoh of Egypt and to set him free as a son of His. He calls him to Himself that he may receive Him as a father, and takes him by the hands like a nurse full of tenderness to teach him to walk in the way of truth, bandages every wound in his depths that struck him during his bondage, draws him with cords of compassion and binds him with the bond of love, and lifts him like a child to caress him with His gentle cheeks, and stretches out His hand to him to feed him Himself... What surpassing tenderness! He plays the part of a nurse full of tenderness toward the human soul, not leaving it in need of anything until He leads it from weak infancy to maturity.

11.0.2.en: In greater detail we follow the words of the Lord Himself, who says:

11.0.3.en: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt" [1]. While Israel was a child or a boy who does not understand things, unable to offer anything on his part, God loved him and called him out of the land of bondage, offering him sonship. So also God loved Jacob while he was still in the womb, having done neither good nor evil (Rom 9:11). As the Lord says to Jeremiah the prophet: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jer 1:5), and the Apostle Paul affirms that God "first loved us."

11.0.4.en: God took the initiative and loved His child Israel and released him from the bondage of Pharaoh, but Israel remained in his heart attached to bondage, like the sick man who loves sickness, or the prisoner who does not depart in his heart from the darkness of the prison. So our Lord Jesus Christ released us from the bondage of the devil, the true Pharaoh, granting us through Baptism sonship to the Father in Him, but often our heart returns to the land of bondage and we long for the leeks and onions of Egypt, as the children of Israel did before, when they wept, saying: "We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick: but now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes" (Num 11:5-6). Their souls dried up from the manna that came down from above, and they longed for the small free fish and the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic! No wonder, for when man attaches himself to the earth he becomes earth, and his soul wearies of heavenly things and longs for earthly things; he sees dryness in the heavenly and pleasure and joy of heart in the earthly.

11.0.5.en: The Evangelist Matthew saw in the divine saying "Out of Egypt have I called my son" a clear and explicit prophecy of the flight of the Lord Christ, the Son of the living God, to our Egypt, which was at that time one of the greatest centers of the Gentiles, to declare His acceptance of all the Gentile peoples, sanctifying our land, so that what was formerly a center of paganism became a place of rest for the Savior of the world. And the Lord still enters our inner Egypt to turn it from its paganism into a sanctuary for Him, in which He sets up His divine altar (Isa 19:19), so that it knows Him and offers Him sacrifice and an offering of love (Isa 19:21), to hear His divine voice: "Blessed be Egypt my people" (Isa 19:25).

11.1.0.en: We return once more to God's care for His child Israel, whom He called from the land of bondage as a son to Him, to learn the son's attitude toward this care. "As they called them, so they went from them: they sacrificed unto Baalim, and burned incense to graven images" [2]. The Septuagint gives it more clearly, declaring that whenever He called them they went away from before Him, as though they were the stubborn son whom his father calls, offering him every protection, but he refuses and flees from his father's face to his enemy, "Baalim and graven images." From his childhood Israel was stubborn toward God, meeting love with coldness and care with obstinacy. Yet God did not cease from His love, for He says: "I taught Ephraim also to go (taught him to walk), taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them" [3]. He tends them like a nurse who takes the hands of the resisting child to teach him how to walk so that he may become mature. He is loving toward them: "I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them" [4]. The Septuagint makes clear that He used to lift them like a child to His cheeks and bend down to put the food into their mouths; what love is greater than this? He offered every care as a father so that we may take refuge in Him and He may enter into us, and we may become one with Him. As St. Jerome says: [Christ stands every day at the door of our heart, longing to enter. Let us open our heart to Him wide, and He will enter and be our guest, dwell in us and sup with us.]

11.2.0.en: 5 "He shall not return into the land of Egypt, but the Assyrian shall be his king, because they refused to return. 6 And the sword shall abide on his cities, and shall consume his branches, and devour them, because of their own counsels. 7 And my people are bent to backsliding from me: though they called them to the most High, none at all would exalt him. 8 How shall I make thee, Ephraim? how shall I set thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me, my mercies are kindled together.

11.2.1.en: "He shall not return into the land of Egypt, but the Assyrian shall be his king" [5]. When Israel met with coldness the care of God, who brought him out of the land of bondage, he longed to return again to the land of bondage to take shelter under the shadow of Pharaoh from the king of Assyria, but even if he flees he will be taken captive under the rule of Assyria, and Assyria will reign over him. This is a picture of mankind's attitude toward God, who calls them in His love, and they disobey Him: they went away from before Him [2], giving Him the back, not the face. Instead of offering Him sacrifices of love they "sacrificed unto Baalim," that is, they sacrifice to one Baal and then return to sacrifice to another and a third, and so on, and do not think of returning to God. So He rebukes them bitterly, saying: "My people are bent (clinging) to backsliding from me"; within them is a strong inclination and attraction toward apostasy. I sent to them those who call them to Me, but they refused to return [5]. In the face of this resistance on Israel's part, God is compelled to discipline, saying: "How shall I make thee, Ephraim? how shall I set thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim?" [8]. He makes Ephraim and Israel like Admah and Zeboim, two cities in the region of Sodom and Gomorrah that were burned with fire because of their evil.

11.3.0.en: 9 "I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not come in wrath. 10 They shall walk after the LORD: he shall roar like a lion: for he shall roar, and the children shall hasten from the west. 11 They shall hasten as a bird out of Egypt, and as a dove out of the land of Assyria: and I will place them in their houses, saith the LORD. 12 Ephraim compasseth me about with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit: but Judah yet strayeth from God, and from the faithful Holy One.

11.3.1.en: Even in moments of discipline God cannot bear to see His people suffering, for His tender heart turns within Him and the fire of His mercies is kindled in Him, and He is bound to remove the fierceness of His anger from them, saying: "Mine heart is turned within me, my mercies are kindled together. I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not come in wrath" [8-9].

11.4.0.en: If He roars like a lion to discipline firmly [10], His sons hasten to flee, as to Pharaoh of Egypt or the king of Assyria, but in His mercies He returns them, not by their strength nor by their sword, but He returns them in their weakness and helplessness, for "they shall hasten as a bird out of Egypt, and as a dove out of the land of Assyria: and I will place them in their houses, saith the LORD" [11]. By His love He returns them to their houses, so that they return like a bird that has no power or strength, or like a simple dove hastened from the land of enemies to its home. He is the refuge of the weak... He protects the sparrow and supports the dove!
